outcome: No polynomial-time algorithm for unknot recognition is established or ruled out as of 13 October 2026. The main new item since January 2024 is Lackenby's arXiv:2607.23350 (posted 25 July 2026), which gives an algorithm deciding whether a knot is trivial (Corollary 1.2) but states no running-time bound in the text read, and claims neither polynomial nor quasi-polynomial time; an AI-generated referee review on Pith reports omitted proofs and no human review. Lackenby's February 2021 quasi-polynomial announcement had no written argument public until that 2026 posting, and an unverified 2025 Zenodo record claims a polynomial-time algorithm.
problem_asks: Whether unknots can be recognized in polynomial time. Unpacked: (1) the decision problem UNKNOT RECOGNITION: given a knot in a standard representation, decide whether it is the unknot; (2) the time bound: whether an algorithm exists whose running time is polynomial in the size of the input, with the statement naming no representation (crossing number of a diagram is the usual measure); (3) the yes/no answer to whether UNKNOT RECOGNITION lies in P. Background the statement does not ask for: decidability (Haken, 1961), membership in NP and in coNP (both known; see events), and quasi-polynomial bounds, which fall short of what is asked.

events.what_happened: Wolfgang Haken's normal-surface algorithm decides whether a knot is the unknot; it is the first algorithm for the problem, first posed by Dehn in 1910. Per the Oxford news item, Haken's algorithm is from 1961 (search results also give Acta Mathematica 1961, 'Theorie der Normalflächen', not opened). Its running time is not polynomial. Lackenby's 2026 paper cites it as the first algorithmic solution.
events.delivers: A decision procedure for unknottedness (decidability). No polynomial running-time bound.
events.remains: The polynomial-time question (the whole of the problem's part (2) and (3)).
events.direction: Decidability only. Cuts toward the problem being decidable, not toward or against polynomial time.

events.what_happened: Hass, Lagarias and Pippenger, 'The Computational Complexity of Knot and Link Problems' (arXiv math/9807016, submitted 3 July 1998; preliminary version FOCS 1997; full version J. ACM 46 (1999), per search results). They show that the unknotting problem is in NP, using normal surfaces and Haken's decision procedures, with exponential worst-case deterministic bounds.
events.revisions: Single version v1 on the arXiv abstract page (opened 13 Oct 2026). J. ACM 1999 publication per search results, DOI not opened.
events.delivers: Unknottedness is in NP. Deterministic algorithms with exponential worst-case bounds. Places the problem in NP, not in P.
events.remains: Polynomial-time question; coNP membership (later, see Kuperberg 2011 and Lackenby 2016).

checked_by.what_they_did: Published the full version, J. ACM 46 (1999), pp. 185-211 (per search results; DOI not opened)

events.direction: Cuts toward NP membership (a checkable yes-certificate). Says nothing about P.

events.what_happened: Hara, Tani and Yamamoto claimed at SODA 2005 ('Unknotting is in AM ∩ co-AM', pp. 359-365, per a publication list in search results) that unknottedness lies in AM ∩ co-AM. The authors later retracted the claim, per the Wikipedia article (fetched). Wikipedia cites this as a personal communication.
events.delivers: Claimed AM ∩ co-AM membership. Withdrawn, so it establishes nothing.
events.doubts: Retracted by the authors. The retraction date and the error found are not established in any source I opened.
events.direction: Would have placed the problem in AM ∩ co-AM. Withdrawn, so cuts neither way.

events.what_happened: Kuperberg, 'Knottedness is in NP, modulo GRH' (arXiv:1112.0845, v1 5 Dec 2011; v2 1 Jan 2014, a minor update). Under the generalized Riemann hypothesis, a short checkable certificate of knottedness exists, so unknot recognition is in coNP under GRH. Combined with Hass-Lagarias-Pippenger, this gives NP ∩ coNP under GRH.
events.revisions: v1 5 Dec 2011; v2 1 Jan 2014 (per arXiv abstract page, opened).
events.delivers: Unknot recognition is in coNP, conditionally on GRH (so NP ∩ coNP under GRH). A complexity-class result, not a polynomial algorithm.
events.remains: Unconditional coNP membership (Lackenby 2016); the polynomial-time question.
events.doubts: Conditional on GRH; the abstract says GRH is needed only to find a short certificate, not to check one.
events.direction: Cuts toward NP ∩ coNP membership under GRH. Says nothing about P.

events.what_happened: Burton and Ozlen, 'A fast branching algorithm for unknot recognition with experimental polynomial-time behaviour' (arXiv:1211.1079, v1 5 Nov 2012; v2 11 Apr 2013; v3 9 Oct 2014). A conclusive branch-and-bound method, using normal surfaces and integer/linear programming, implemented in Regina. The abstract says it is exponential in theory but shows polynomial-time behaviour under exhaustive experiments, covering all 2977 non-trivial prime knots with at most 12 crossings.
events.revisions: v1 5 Nov 2012; v2 11 Apr 2013; v3 9 Oct 2014 (per arXiv abstract page, opened). The comment field says 'To appear in Mathematical Programming'; the journal version was not opened.
events.delivers: A conclusive unknot-recognition algorithm with exponential worst case and experimentally polynomial-looking behaviour on the tested knots. No proof of a polynomial bound.
events.direction: Empirical. Cuts neither way on worst-case polynomial time; the abstract itself says the worst case is exponential.

events.what_happened: Lackenby, 'A polynomial upper bound on Reidemeister moves' (arXiv:1302.0180, v1 1 Feb 2013; v2 11 Dec 2014; Annals of Mathematics 182 (2015), per the Wikipedia reference list). Any diagram of the unknot with c crossings can be reduced to the trivial diagram using at most (236c)^11 Reidemeister moves.
events.revisions: v1 1 Feb 2013; v2 11 Dec 2014 (per arXiv abstract page, opened). Annals of Mathematics 2015, DOI 10.4007/annals.2015.182.2.3 (per Wikipedia reference list, not opened).
events.delivers: A polynomial bound on the length of unknotting sequences for c-crossing unknot diagrams. The abstract gives no algorithm or running time for recognition. A search summary says the paper notes this gives a polynomial-time certificate of unknottedness; not checked in the text.
events.remains: A running time for a decision algorithm, and whether a polynomial-time method can find such a sequence (open).

checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper, Annals 182(2) 2015 (per Wikipedia reference list)

events.direction: A bound on move counts, not on algorithm time. Neither cuts toward nor against polynomial recognition; it is an ingredient for the NP certificate.

events.what_happened: Lackenby, 'The efficient certification of knottedness and Thurston norm' (arXiv:1604.00290, v1 1 Apr 2016; v2 10 Jul 2019; v3 12 Apr 2021, which the comments say is to appear in Advances in Mathematics; journal reference 2021 per Wikipedia). The abstract says: 'We show that the problem of determining whether a knot in the 3-sphere is non-trivial lies in NP.' With no GRH hypothesis, this gives unknot recognition in coNP, so NP ∩ coNP unconditionally.
events.revisions: v1 1 Apr 2016; v2 10 Jul 2019; v3 12 Apr 2021 (per arXiv abstract page, opened). Advances in Mathematics 387 (2021), DOI 10.1016/j.aim.2021.107796 (per Wikipedia; not opened).
events.delivers: Knottedness is in NP unconditionally, hence unknot recognition is in coNP unconditionally. Complexity-class membership only; no polynomial algorithm.

checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted the paper for publication in 2021 (v3 comment 'to appear'; journal reference per Wikipedia)

events.direction: Cuts toward NP ∩ coNP membership, unconditionally. Says nothing about P.

events.what_happened: Baldwin and Sivek, 'On the complexity of torus knot recognition' (arXiv:1706.04424, v1 14 Jun 2017; v2 6 Sep 2017). Recognizing a diagram of a specific torus knot, or of any torus knot, is in NP ∩ coNP, assuming GRH.
events.revisions: v1 14 Jun 2017; v2 6 Sep 2017 ('reorganized section 2, other minor changes', per arXiv abstract page, opened).
events.delivers: Restricted to torus knots, and conditional on GRH. The abstract does not say whether the unknot is covered.
events.remains: The general unknot problem, and the polynomial-time question.
events.doubts: Restricted class and conditional on GRH.
events.direction: Restricted class (torus knots), conditional. Cuts toward NP ∩ coNP for torus knots only; a different class from the problem.

events.what_happened: Meesum and Prathamesh, 'Unknot Recognition Through Quantifier Elimination' (arXiv:1803.00413, submitted 27 Feb 2018). Encodes unknot recognition as a validity problem in the existential theory of real closed fields, using SU(2) representations of knot groups (Kronheimer-Mrowka), and gives an algorithm of complexity 2^O(n), n the crossing number, which the abstract says matches the best known unknot recognition runtimes.
events.revisions: Single version v1 (per arXiv abstract page, opened).
events.delivers: An exponential algorithm, 2^O(n) in crossings. No polynomial claim.
events.direction: Exponential-time algorithm. Cuts neither way on polynomial time. No engagement found in this search; citation trail not checked.

events.what_happened: de Mesmay, Rieck, Sedgwick and Tancer, 'The unbearable hardness of unknotting' (arXiv:1810.03502, v1 8 Oct 2018; SoCG 2019 per search results). Deciding whether a diagram of the unknot can be untangled using at most k Reidemeister moves, with k part of the input, is NP-hard. Search results attribute this to Demaine; the opened arXiv page lists the four authors above.
events.revisions: Single version v1 (per arXiv abstract page, opened).
events.delivers: NP-hardness of untangling a given unknot diagram within a move budget k given as input. A different problem from unknot recognition: the input includes a move budget, and the diagram is already known to be the unknot.
events.remains: Unknot recognition itself, which this result does not address.
events.direction: A neighbouring problem (move-bounded untangling). Cuts toward NP-hardness of that task; does not decide recognition.

events.what_happened: Gukov, Halverson, Ruehle and Sułkowski, 'Learning to Unknot' (arXiv:2010.16263, v1 28 Oct 2020; later published in 2021 per a Caltech record in search results). Treats UNKNOT as binary classification of closures of random braid words with transformer networks (Reformer and shared-QK Transformer outperform fully-connected networks, at ≳95% accuracy), and uses reinforcement learning to find explicit sequences of Markov moves and braid relations that unknot diagrams, giving a certificate per knot. The abstract does not present a polynomial-time decision procedure.
events.revisions: v1 28 Oct 2020; no later version on the arXiv page (opened). Journal publication 21 April 2021 per Caltech record (search result, not opened).
events.delivers: Empirical classifiers for unknottedness on braid closures up to the tested crossing numbers, and RL-produced unknotting sequences that certify unknottedness for individual knots. Not a general algorithm and not a complexity bound.
events.remains: A general decision procedure with a complexity bound; the polynomial-time question.

checked_by.who: IOP Publishing journal (name not confirmed in the sources read; Machine Learning: Science and Technology is a guess from the publisher, not verified)
checked_by.qualification: Journal of record; refereed (publisher's standard process, not verified by opening the journal)
checked_by.what_they_did: Published (accepted 23 Feb 2021; published 21 Apr 2021, per Caltech record in search results)

events.doubts: Classifier accuracy is empirical and gives probabilities, not proofs. RL certificates cover individual knots, not the general problem.
events.direction: Heuristic and certificate-producing methods on the problem's family of inputs. Does not cut toward P or against it.
events.object: No single object. The RL method produces explicit unknotting sequences of Markov moves and braid relations for individual unknot braid closures, which can be checked directly as certificates.

systems.name: Reformer
systems.what_it_did: A transformer-type network architecture trained to classify braid-word closures as unknot or not; the authors report it outperforms fully-connected networks.
systems.basis_quote: We find that the Reformer and shared-QK Transformer network architectures outperform fully-connected networks,

systems.name: shared-QK Transformer
systems.what_it_did: A transformer-type network architecture trained to classify braid-word closures as unknot or not; the authors report it outperforms fully-connected networks.
systems.basis_quote: We find that the Reformer and shared-QK Transformer network architectures outperform fully-connected networks,

systems.name: Trust region policy optimization (TRPO)
systems.what_it_did: A reinforcement learning method used to find sequences of Markov moves and braid relations that simplify knots to the unknot; the output is an explicit unknotting sequence for each knot.
systems.basis_quote: Trust region policy optimization (TRPO) performs consistently well for a wide range of crossing numbers

events.what_happened: Lackenby announced an unknot recognition algorithm that runs in quasi-polynomial time: 'the algorithm decides whether a knot is the unknot in n^{c log(n)} steps, for some constant c' (Oxford Mathematics news item, posted 2 February 2021). It was first outlined at a UC Davis seminar on 2 February 2021, per the same item, with a recording and slides linked. The slides ('Unknot recognition in quasi-polynomial time', dated February 2021 on his Oxford page) could not be read as text. Later talks restate the claim with a different running-time form: a Princeton talk on 15 April 2021 and a Tsinghua talk on 7 November 2024 both give 2^O((log n)^3) for a diagram with n crossings. Press coverage in New Scientist and on BBC World Service is reported by the St Catherine's College item (not opened). No written argument for the claim was found before the 2026 arXiv posting (see lackenby-2026-arxiv-2607-23350).
events.revisions: Restated in talks 15 Apr 2021 (Princeton) and 7 Nov 2024 (Tsinghua, online), with running time 2^O((log n)^3). Not published in a peer-reviewed venue as of October 2025, per the Wikipedia article (fetched). The 2026 arXiv paper does not state a quasi-polynomial bound in the text read.
events.delivers: As announced: a decision procedure for unknottedness running in n^{O(log n)} (or 2^O((log n)^3)) steps in the crossing number. Restricted to quasi-polynomial time; no polynomial claim. No argument public, so what it establishes cannot be checked.
events.remains: Whether the problem admits a polynomial-time algorithm, which quasi-polynomial time does not settle.
events.doubts: Unpublished for over five years on the Wikipedia account. No written argument public until the 2026 posting. The running-time form changes between the announcement (n^{c log n}) and the talk abstracts (2^O((log n)^3)). The 2026 paper, the latest written work, does not state a quasi-polynomial bound in the text read, and its Section 9 says some steps' running time is not estimated. The 2021 slides could not be read, so I cannot tell whether they contain an argument.
events.direction: Claims a quasi-polynomial decision procedure. If accepted, the problem's answer would be 'quasi-polynomial, not known to be polynomial'. It does not decide the polynomial-time question.

events.what_happened: A self-published Zenodo record titled 'Unknotting problem' (record 15460941; search results describe it as version 3 published 18 May 2025 and as asserting 'a complete solution with a polynomial-time decision algorithm', running in time O(c(K)^5) in the crossing number, via a self-adjoint resonance operator on the knot configuration space). I could not open the record: the fetch returned HTTP 504 on five attempts. The description above is from a search-result summary and is not verified.
events.revisions: Version 3 dated 18 May 2025 per search results; the same results say a newer version exists (not inspected).
events.delivers: Claimed: a polynomial-time decision algorithm for unknottedness, O(c^5). Not checked. If the claim held, it would answer the problem affirmatively.
events.remains: Unknown; the claim could not be read.
events.doubts: Self-published upload. Search results found no journal, arXiv posting, expert review, or verification. Per the same search summary, the record reports numerical validation only and reuses constants that it says appear in other claimed solutions; this is unverified because the record was not opened. The Wikipedia article (fetched) and the 2026 Lackenby paper's context treat the problem as open.
events.direction: Claims an affirmative answer: a polynomial-time algorithm, so it would cut toward P. Unverified.
events.object: Per a search-result summary only: a decision algorithm built from a self-adjoint resonance operator on the knot configuration space, whose stability functional is maximal exactly when the knot is the unknot. Not checked.

events.what_happened: Applebaum, Blackwell, Davies, Edlich, Juhász, Lackenby, Tomašev and Zheng (Google DeepMind and Oxford), 'The unknotting number, hard unknot diagrams, and reinforcement learning' (arXiv:2409.09032, v1 13 Sept 2024; v2 19 July 2025). A reinforcement learning agent finds minimal sequences of crossing changes that unknot diagrams with up to 200 crossings; this gives upper bounds on the unknotting number, used to determine the unknotting number of 57k knots and, assuming additivity, of 43 knots with at most 12 crossings. A by-product is a dataset of 2.6 million distinct hard unknot diagrams, most under 35 crossings.
events.revisions: v1 13 Sep 2024; v2 19 Jul 2025 (per arXiv abstract page, opened). Oxford ORA record lists it as a journal article (not opened).
events.delivers: Upper bounds on the unknotting number of many knots, and a dataset of hard unknot diagrams. The 43-knot values rest on an assumed additivity of the unknotting number. This is about the unknotting number, a different quantity from unknot recognition; it gives no recognition algorithm and no complexity bound for recognition.

checked_by.qualification: Institutional repository record; not a review
checked_by.what_they_did: Lists the paper as a journal article; the journal was not opened

events.directly_checkable: The 2.6 million hard unknot diagrams are an object anyone could check by running a simplification; the dataset's location was not found in the sources read.
events.doubts: The 43-knot values are conditional on assumed additivity of the unknotting number, as the authors state. This is a stated condition, not a doubt about the result.
events.direction: Upper bounds on the unknotting number, which is a neighbouring question. Cuts neither way on unknot recognition.
events.object: A dataset of 2.6 million hard unknot diagrams (most under 35 crossings), and sequences of crossing changes unknotting diagrams of up to 200 crossings, with which upper bounds on unknotting number were obtained for 57k knots. Explicit or computed; not checked by me.

systems.name: a reinforcement learning agent
systems.what_it_did: Found minimal sequences of crossing changes that unknot diagrams (up to 200 crossings), used for the unknotting-number upper bounds and the 2.6 million hard unknot diagram dataset. The abstract gives no product name; the IMPALA architecture named in a 2023 conference abstract by Juhász is not in the paper's abstract and is not recorded here as the system's name.
systems.basis_quote: We have developed a reinforcement learning agent that often finds a minimal sequence of unknotting crossing changes

events.what_happened: Dranowski, Kabkov and Tubbenhauer, 'RL unknotter, hard unknots and unknotting number' (arXiv:2603.07955; v1 9 Mar 2026; v2 5 Apr 2026; v3 29 Apr 2026; v4 9 Sep 2026). A reinforcement learning pipeline (the 'unknotter') for simplifying knot diagrams, tested on 'very hard' unknot diagrams; uses diagram inflation to study the upper bound of three for the unknotting number of 4_1#9_10; a self-improving extension improves unknotting-number upper bounds on prime knots. The abstract makes no claim of a new unknot recognition method or a polynomial-time result.
events.revisions: v1 9 Mar 2026; v2 5 Apr 2026; v3 29 Apr 2026; v4 9 Sep 2026 (per arXiv abstract page, opened).
events.delivers: Simplification trajectories for hard unknot diagrams, and upper bounds on the unknotting number. Not a recognition complexity result. Neighbouring question.
events.direction: Upper bounds on the unknotting number and practical simplification. Cuts neither way on the complexity of unknot recognition. No engagement found beyond index results.
events.object: No new object beyond the diagram-inflation analysis of 4_1#9_10 and a pipeline that produces unknotting sequences for prime knots.

systems.name: PPO as implemented in stable-baselines3
systems.what_it_did: Trains the 'unknotter' agent, which finds simplification trajectories for diagrams (macro-actions in a gymnasium environment whose states are diagrams).
systems.basis_quote: We train neural agents that, when run from a given diagram, reliably find simplification trajectories.

events.what_happened: Cantarella, Schumacher and Shonkwiler, 'Hard unknots are often easy from a different perspective' (arXiv:2607.28772; v1 30 Jul 2026; v2 23 Sep 2026; v3 6 Oct 2026). Introduces ReAPR, a semi-diagrammatic simplifier that alternates pass-move reduction with geometric re-embedding. Proves the minimum total variation for an n-crossing diagram is 2(n-k), with k the least number of crossings that must be virtualized to make it virtually alternating. Reports simplifying about 2.6 million hard-unknot examples in under 30 seconds of total CPU time, and says ReAPR is as effective as the best non-diagrammatic unknot recognition method (SnapPy) and about 60x faster. v3 says it updated timings with improved Regina methods and that theorems and ReAPR results are unchanged.
events.revisions: v1 30 Jul 2026; v2 23 Sep 2026; v3 6 Oct 2026, timings updated, 'No changes to theorems or ReAPR results.' (per arXiv abstract page, opened).
events.delivers: A practical simplifier that empirically reduces the published hard-unknot examples, plus a theorem on minimum total variation for n-crossing diagrams. It has no worst-case running-time result stated in the abstract, so it does not decide unknottedness in polynomial time.
events.remains: Worst-case complexity of unknot recognition (not addressed).
events.direction: Practical performance and a diagram-level theorem. Cuts neither toward P nor against it.
events.object: ReAPR, an algorithm (simplifier) rather than an object. Its total-variation theorem concerns n-crossing diagrams.

events.what_happened: Lackenby, 'Incompressible surfaces, hierarchies and unknot recognition' (arXiv:2607.23350, math.GT, 54 pages; v1 submitted 25 July 2026, the only version listed when checked on 13 Oct 2026). Gives an algorithm deciding whether a compact orientable surface properly embedded in a compact orientable 3-manifold is incompressible; Corollary 1.2 states: 'There is an algorithm to determine whether a given knot in the 3-sphere is trivial.' The abstract also claims a new proof that deciding whether a compact orientable 3-manifold has incompressible boundary is in NP. The text read gives no running-time bound for the unknot algorithm. Section 9 gives an iteration bound L(g+1)^L; Section 10 gives a linear bound on L (Proposition 10.2: partial hierarchy length at most 4c_q(ℋ)). Section 9 says some steps are 'not described with enough precision to be able to estimate their running time'. The paper does not state the quasi-polynomial bound from the 2021 announcement in the text read. Funding: EPSRC EP/Y004256/1.
events.revisions: v1 25 Jul 2026 only (as of 13 Oct 2026). A Pith review of 31 Jul 2026 refers to this version.
events.delivers: A decision algorithm for trivial knots (Corollary 1.2) as a special case of incompressibility, with no running-time bound stated in the text read. Also a new proof of NP membership for incompressible boundary (per the abstract), which the abstract connects to the unknot case. Per a search summary (not checked in the text), a knot exterior has incompressible boundary exactly when the knot is non-trivial, which would make the unknot case a special case; the 2016 Lackenby result already gives knottedness in NP. Does not claim polynomial or quasi-polynomial time.
events.remains: Whether unknot recognition is in P; the running time of the unknot algorithm (not stated, and Section 9 declines to estimate several steps); whether the 2021 quasi-polynomial claim holds, which this paper does not address in the text read.

checked_by.who: Pith (AI referee review, generated by 'deepseek-v4-flash', 31 July 2026)
checked_by.qualification: None: the page states 'This review was written by an AI. No human expert has reviewed this paper yet.'
checked_by.what_they_did: Wrote a review with the verdict 'A substantial algorithmic 3-manifold paper with a genuinely new NP/co-NP result, but the NP certificate rests on an omitted proof that needs to be supplied.' Recommends sending the paper out with the omitted proofs supplied.

events.doubts: (1) Omitted proofs: the paper states Theorem 14.4 (cutting along a surface) and says 'It has essentially the same proof, which is omitted'. I confirmed this sentence in the text. The Pith review reports that Theorem 12.3 is also omitted with 'essentially the same' wording, that Theorem 14.1's verification argument is unproven, and that the NP certificate's polynomial-time guarantee is unsupported without Theorem 14.4; I did not check those claims in the text. (2) Section 9 says some steps are 'not described with enough precision to be able to estimate their running time' (confirmed in the text). (3) The Pith review lists minor errors (an incorrect statement in Lemma 3.5, a duplicated passage in the proof of Theorem 13.1, a typesetting error in Definition 5.1); not checked. (4) The 2021 quasi-polynomial bound is not in this paper, so the paper does not say whether it supports that claim. (5) The only written review found is AI-generated; no human review found as of 13 Oct 2026.
events.direction: An algorithm for trivial knots with no complexity bound stated in the text read. Does not claim polynomial or quasi-polynomial time, so as far as the text read it does not move a stated bound on the complexity of unknot recognition.
events.object: A decision procedure for whether a knot in the 3-sphere is trivial, built from hierarchies and handle structures of normal surfaces (Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 1.2). It is an algorithm, not an exhibited object; its running time is not stated in the text read.

disputes.summary: Search summaries conflict with the fetched source on the Epoch benchmark. Summaries say GPT-5.2 Pro solved the 'warm-up' (unknot detection, unknotting number zero) of Epoch's 'Deciding Unknotting Number One' problem and that Gemini 3 Deep Think did not solve the full problem. The Epoch page fetched on 13 Oct 2026 lists no model attempts or results, describes no warm-up section, and records removal from the benchmark on 2026-07-31. Not recorded as an event; the claim is unverified.

Running-time forms differ across Lackenby's 2021 statements: the Oxford news item gives n^{c log n} steps; the Princeton (15 Apr 2021) and Tsinghua (7 Nov 2024) abstracts give 2^O((log n)^3) for n crossings. The 2026 arXiv paper states neither in the text read. Recorded in events, not resolved.

Search summaries misattribute or misdate several items, corrected from primary sources opened here. Demaine is named in a search query, but the 2018 k-move NP-hardness paper's authors are de Mesmay, Rieck, Sedgwick and Tancer. A Lean-search summary gives Haken's decision result as 1962; the Oxford news item gives 1961. One summary says the 2025 He–Sedgwick–Spreer paper and the 2025 Cheng et al. paper treat unknot recognition as open or cite Lackenby; the opened abstracts of both do neither (recorded in the summary, not as events).

summary: No source found settles whether unknot recognition is in P. The main new item is Lackenby's arXiv:2607.23350 (25 July 2026), which gives an algorithm deciding whether a knot is trivial (Corollary 1.2). The text I read states no running-time bound, claims neither polynomial nor quasi-polynomial time, and says in Section 9 that some steps are 'not described with enough precision to be able to estimate their running time'; its Theorem 14.4 is stated with its proof omitted ('It has essentially the same proof, which is omitted'), which I confirmed in the text. The only written review I found is an AI-generated referee report on Pith (generated by 'deepseek-v4-flash', 31 July 2026), which says no human expert has reviewed the paper and reports omitted proofs and an unsupported polynomial-time guarantee for the NP certificate; I did not verify its other objections. The 2026 paper does not state the quasi-polynomial bound from Lackenby's February 2021 announcement (Oxford news: n^{c log n} steps; Princeton talk of 15 April 2021 and Tsinghua talk of 7 November 2024 abstracts: 2^O((log n)^3)). Whether the 2021 claim should be dated to the 2026 write-up is a close call under §5.1: the Oxford item is a claim rather than an argument, and the February 2021 slides could not be read as text, so both events are recorded separately for the later pass. Wikipedia (fetched; 'as of October 2025') says the 2021 result is unpublished in peer-reviewed literature. A self-published Zenodo record (search snippet: version 3, 18 May 2025) asserts a polynomial-time algorithm of order c^5; the record returned HTTP 504 on five attempts, so I could not read it, and no expert engagement turned up. Older events: Haken (1961, decidability), Hass–Lagarias–Pippenger (NP, 1998), Hara–Tani–Yamamoto (AM ∩ co-AM, 2005, retracted), Kuperberg (coNP under GRH, 2011), Burton–Ozlen (experimentally polynomial, exponential worst case, 2012), Lackenby (polynomial Reidemeister bound, 2013; knottedness in NP unconditionally, 2016), Baldwin–Sivek (torus knots, GRH, 2017), Meesum–Prathamesh (2^O(n) quantifier elimination, 2018), de Mesmay et al. (NP-hard move-bounded untangling, 2018, a different problem). AI searches found AI only in neighbouring or earlier work: Gukov et al. (2020) transformer classifiers and TRPO certificates for individual knots; the DeepMind–Oxford RL agent (2024) for unknotting number, with a dataset of 2.6 million hard unknot diagrams; and Dranowski et al. (2026) RL unknotter using PPO as implemented in stable-baselines3, for unknotting-number bounds. No AI system was found in the 2026 Lackenby paper, the 2026 Cantarella–Schumacher–Shonkwiler simplifier (abstract read only), or the 2021 announcement. Close calls: (a) the 2021 announcement's dating; (b) whether the 2026 paper completes a quasi-polynomial bound (not stated in what I read; Section 9 leaves some steps unanalysed); (c) whether the Zenodo claim matters (unread). Search summaries claimed a GPT-5.2 Pro warm-up solution and a 2025 link between Lackenby's claim and later papers; the sources I opened do not support them, so I recorded neither as events.
competing_reading: The strongest case for a settled quasi-polynomial status: the 2021 announcement is the real result and the 2026 paper is its write-up. Oxford, Princeton and Tsinghua all present the quasi-polynomial algorithm as the result, and the Pith review calls the 2026 paper a 'genuinely new NP/co-NP result'. Under §5.1 a talk is dated to its write-up, which would move the claim to July 2026 and make it a quasi-polynomial algorithm on the record. Against this, the 2026 text as read states no running-time bound, says some steps are not analysed, and omits proofs, so the quasi-polynomial bound is not on the page. A reading in which the Zenodo polynomial claim is a real solution has no support beyond the search snippet; the record was not read, no expert engagement was found, and Wikipedia treats the problem as open.
what_would_settle_it: (a) A readable copy of the Zenodo record 15460941 (the fetch returned 504 five times) and any expert reading of its O(c^5) algorithm. (b) The full running-time analysis in arXiv:2607.23350: the steps Section 9 declines to estimate, and the proofs of Theorems 12.3 and 14.4 that Pith reports as omitted; a stated quasi-polynomial or polynomial bound would settle that the 2026 paper carries the 2021 claim. (c) The text of the February 2021 slides (the PDF on Lackenby's page is binary to the fetch tool here), to decide whether they are a written argument and therefore fix the 2021 event's date. (d) Journal acceptance or expert verification of arXiv:2607.23350, or of the 2021 claim. (e) Any published response by Lackenby to the Pith objections, or a later citation of the 2026 paper that restates a running-time bound.

incomplete: (1) The Zenodo record 15460941 could not be opened (HTTP 504 on five fetch attempts and one search); its content is described only from a search summary, and its creator is unknown. (2) The February 2021 slides ('quasipolynomial-talk.pdf') are a binary PDF whose text the fetch tool could not read; the saved copy lies outside the main directory, so I did not open it locally. The 2021 event's dating under §5.1 therefore rests on the Oxford item and is a close call. (3) The arXiv 2607.28772 PDF and HTML were unreadable or not found (404/binary); only its abstract was read, so its acknowledgements and any AI mention in the body were not checked and its none_found is provisional. (4) The arXiv 2607.23350 text was read in three chunks (0–100k, 100k–200k, 200k–228k). The 100k–200k chunk was read for running-time content and then scanned for AI mentions; the first and last chunks were checked for AI mentions and omitted proofs. The Pith review's further objections (Theorems 12.3 and 14.1, Lemma 3.5, the Theorem 13.1 duplicate, Definition 5.1) were not verified in the text. (5) Wikipedia was read through a summarising fetch, so quotes are paraphrased and the 'as of October 2025' wording is as the summariser reported it. (6) The Kyoto 2025 slides (404), the tagteam blog (HTTP 503), the Epoch PDF (binary), and the Princeton listing node/17460 were not read. (7) The Oct 2024 Oxford OMI talk and the New Scientist and BBC items were not opened. (8) Journal details for Haken 1961 (Acta Mathematica), Hass–Lagarias–Pippenger (J. ACM 1999), Burton–Ozlen (Mathematical Programming), Learning to Unknot (IOP, 2021), and Lackenby 2016 (Advances in Mathematics 2021) are from search results or Wikipedia and were not checked at the journal. (9) Checking for later work citing the 2021 claim, the 2026 arXiv paper, or the Zenodo record was limited: the 2026 paper is about eleven weeks old, and I did not find a citing paper. (10) Human expert engagement with arXiv:2607.23350 beyond the Pith AI review was not found in search, but I did not search Lackenby's citing papers or mailing lists exhaustively. (11) The HTY 2005 retraction date and reasons are not established. (12) The AI search covered knot and unknot queries and named labs and models; no knot-specific AI result beyond the listed events was found.
